articles.title: Pentagon Accelerates Economic Warfare Strategy to Guard Compute Infrastructure
articles.content: AI chip leader Nvidia launched an investigation into reports CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence campaign—just as the U.S. has intensified its own efforts at economic warfare. Recommended Video Nvidia’s board released a statement Sunday that a committee of independent directors and an outside counsel will oversee the probe, adding that Huang supports the review and plans to cooperate. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said. “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” The announcement followed reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence suspects was working as a spy for China. According to the New York Times and Financial Times , the Nvidia boss admitted to the affair and apologized in an internal message to company employees. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he said in the message. Representatives for Nvidia and Megaspeed didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. U.S. officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, sources told the FT , and surveillance revealed that she was feeding information to China, according to the New York Times . Jensen Huang, who isn’t related to Alice, is a central figure in the U.S. AI industry, leading a company that develops world-class chips powering large language models. Its technology is so sensitive that the Trump administration has restricted exports of Nvidia’s most cutting-edge products to China while President Donald Trump has often cited the U.S.-China AI rivalry as a reason for not slowing down development. Meanwhile, Megaspeed is a Singapore-based data center company that quickly became one of Nvidia’s top customers in Asia, purchasing more than $4.8 billion in chips over the past two years. But the U.S. also investigated Megaspeed last year for allegedly helping smuggle restricted AI chips into China, which the company has denied. News of the Nvidia’s probe into Huang comes weeks after reports indicated the U.S. defense and intelligence communities are getting more aggressive about industrial espionage. Sources told the Washington Post that the Pentagon is planning a spying program that deploys “nonofficial cover officers” who pose as executives—a covert effort in a larger economic warfare campaign. Politico also reported that the Defense Department is quietly building an elite agency to covertly sabotage foreign technology programs that could threaten U.S. military superiority. The Technology Support Office was established in April by reorganizing two classified intelligence programs that have been secretly carrying out technology sabotage at a smaller scale since 2023. The Pentagon has denied the reports. “This query appears to be built on information that is simply not true. Whoever is feeding you these claims are either badly misinformed or deliberately leading you astray to peddle their fantasies,” it told both outlets. But other signs point to the U.S. taking economic warfare more seriously. In September, CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis said the U.S. is expanding espionage against China by targeting companies in sensitive areas like AI, biotechnology and chips. Also this year, the Pentagon formed the Economic Defense Unit for “deterring, denying, disrupting, and helping to defeat adversaries through economic means,” sources told DefenseScoop . AI in particular has emerged as such an important technology that the Defense Department has been more heavy-handed with U.S. companies as well. Anthropic’s AI models were used in the military, but a dispute between the San Francisco-based startup and top brass led to a schism just as the Iran war started. CEO Dario Amodei has said the company is patriotic and seeks to defend the U.S ., but wouldn’t allow its AI to be used in mass domestic surveillance or autonomous weapons. The Pentagon insisted it would use the AI in lawful scenarios and refused to abide by any limits from the company that would go beyond those constraints. After failing to reach a compromise earlier this year, Trump ordered the Pentagon to phase out Anthropic’s technology. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also designated the company a supply-chain risk, meaning contractors can’t use it for military work. Last month, an appeals court ruled the supply-chain risk designation is illegal, but the Pentagon confirmed it’s no longer using any Anthropic tools. articles.title: Algorithmic Caregiving Apps Stumble Against Deepening Eldercare Labor Deficits
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story I are caregivers for our middle son, who has multiple disabilities and requires full-time support. We do our best to keep one another up to date on the activities that fill his daily life while also managing his numerous medical specialists, procedures, and therapies. We have to stay in constant communication while also working our jobs, caring for three teenagers, and managing a household. It’s tough. We’re not alone in our struggles. According to AARP , in 2025, an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability. On average, these caregivers spend up to 27 hours per week providing care. This caregiver crisis, where so many Americans provide ongoing, complex care and, as a result, endure poor health, financial strain, and isolation, is worsening as caregivers need more support and better systems. Helpfully, to lighten the mental load, caregiver apps are aimed at families who are supporting seniors, children, or anyone with a diagnosis that needs regular management. Apps for Different Types of Caregivers Every caregiver’s situation is different, and the apps and programs in this space reflect a diversity of needs. Medisafe , which was created in 2013, tracks medications and sends reminders so users don’t miss a dose. The program can also notify a caregiver if a dose is missed. It gives its users the ability to track medical appointments, track their symptoms, and maintain a list of health care contacts and measurements. It also has a drug interaction checker where users can enter multiple medications to see if they are safe to take at the same time. Caring Village , which was founded in 2015, has an appointment calendar, a to-do list, and a wellness journal where users can keep track of their loved one’s symptoms and moods, and even upload a photo. Caregivers can assign tasks through the app, create a care plan, and receive reminders to take medication. The app also comes with an AI assistant called Julia that can answer caregiving questions. In 2022, Bret Koncak, based on his experiences with his two sons who have complex needs, cocreated Mejo , a web-based caregiver app. Users enter an individual’s medical history, which is then consolidated into a one-page summary that can be shared with caregivers, doctors, and therapists. “A lot of people think that caregiving begins and ends with interactions with the health care system, but a lot of it is about what happens between care visits,” says Koncak. “That's what we're focused on.” For $6 a month or $60 a year, the premium version of Mejo gives users access to daily journaling, which they can share with other caregivers, so everyone stays on the same page without having to catch up verbally. Brett Rowell, whose son Briggs has cerebral palsy, is creating an app called Briggzy , so he and his wife, who work different hours, can more easily hand off their son’s care. Briggzy is currently in the testing phase, and Rowell hopes to launch it to a wider community in 2027. “My wife took [our son] to most of the appointments because I worked 8 to 5 and she was off during that time,” said Rowell. “So the questionnaires alone, I don't know how to answer half of them unless I have Briggzy. My goal was to bring her mind into a shared space for me, so that way I can be helpful.” Nasha Fitter, who has a daughter with a rare disease, launched Citizen Health in 2024 with cofounder Farid Vij to collect medical records for patients and store them in a secure portal. “With the users’ consent, we can extract information from those medical records, deidentify it, harmonize it, and start to pull an understanding of diseases through that,” says Fitter. “And then we feed that understanding back to patients so they would get a better sense of the trajectory of their child’s disease.” Citizen Health works with patient advocacy groups to support their research on drug development. Six months ago, the company launched Ari, an AI “health teammate” that lets caregivers and patients track their loved one's care and symptoms by texting with it. Ari, currently in beta, can also access medical records, patient portals, and Google Calendar events, including specific appointment dates and surgeries. Ari notices caregiver patterns, such as whether they take medication at different times of the day and how that might impact symptoms. It prepares patients and caregivers for appointments by summarizing past medical information and providing appropriate questions to ask medical professionals. And it can help navigate insurance and government benefits. Trying to Lighten the Load I. Glenn Cohen, a bioethics and health law researcher and professor at Harvard Law School, is optimistic about AI in the health space overall. “For example, I think it will empower many patients to prep for questions they might want to ask their doctor before going in to see them.” But he says that users should go into the process with their eyes open to understand the risks and what you're getting out of it, especially if a product is free or cheap. Most of these devices are not medical devices, says Cohen. “As such, the FDA has not reviewed them, so their safety and efficacy remain a question mark, or it's the company's word for it that you have to take.” The health information patients and caregivers plug into these AI tools is not protected by federal HIPAA statutes because the information is typically not coming from a covered entity. Instead, it comes from a person or from data collection at home. “If your privacy is important and you care about how the information is used, in some cases, all you can rely on is the contractual promises,” Cohen says. “They typically have language that absolves [the companies] from responsibility in many instances.” He also warns that the information collected may not be only for the person receiving care, but may also include information about parents or other caregivers. While I love the idea of keeping my son’s information all in one place so I can keep track of patterns, update his doctors without feeling emotionally drained, and easily hand off his caregiving needs to my husband, making sure we update the app regularly will be the key to actually seeing those benefits. , has seen many apps come and go because she says they can be tedious to maintain, especially when caregivers are already overloaded. “We have to upload data to the app (care plans, schedules, tasks), and that’s a lot of work,” Brown says. “A physician, visiting nurse, therapist, or hospital discharge planner won’t log into the app to provide updates, which ends up falling back on the caregiver.” At the end of the day, the need for caregiver apps is great, and many developers in this community, many of whom are caregivers themselves, are trying to do something to lessen the load. “The technology and apps can open the door for broader seamless integration of care—and hopefully less stress on you as the caregiver,” says Nicole Howell, director of direct care workforce development at the National Council on Aging . But she says the final solution [to the overall caregiver crisis] will be something that not one family, not one caregiver can solve. “It has to be all hands at the wheel. It has to be government. It has to be private. It has to be family members speaking up, saying the hard truth so we get the best of American ingenuity to move this to where we need to be.”

articles.title: Amazon Rebuilds Astro Robot Around Embodied Foundation Models
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAmazon has formed a new home robot team and is hiring for a “new-to-world robot product,” according to CNBC’s analysis of job posts.The company has tried to break into the consumer robotics market before with the launch of its $1450 Astro device in 2021, but the product never made it out of beta.Recent advances in artificial intelligence and robotics technology have kickstarted a new wave of humanoid development.In this article Jeff Bezos made a bold bet in 2017. A sci-fi and robotics enthusiast, Bezos was convinced that consumers would have a robot in their home in the not-too-distant future. The Amazon founder and then-CEO told a group of the company's top device executives to get to work on building one, and within a few years, the team came up with the $1,450 Astro. The public got its first look at Astro, essentially an Alexa-equipped tablet on wheels that can autonomously navigate a home, recognize faces and act as a roving security monitor, when it rolled on stage at Amazon's fall 2021 event. But it never evolved beyond an invite-only product. Astro shipped to just a few thousand customers, some of whom now believe the robot's days are numbered. The company also released an Astro for businesses in 2023, before sunsetting it less than a year later. Amazon isn't giving up on Bezos' dream of a household robot just yet, despite its stumbles with Astro. Over the past several months, the company has assembled a new team that's working on a "new-to-world robot product," according to a CNBC analysis of job posts. "Robots are about to step out of the movies and into our homes," a recent job listing for an engineer, which has since been removed, stated. The post details a product capable of navigating "dynamic home environments" and "autonomous operation alongside family members." Amazon is known for making long-term bets at the risk of "being misunderstood" in the short term if it gives the company an early advantage in new markets, like it did with the Alexa voice assistant or Kindle e-reader. CEO Andy Jassy reminded investors of this approach in his latest annual letter, where he said artificial intelligence and robotics were among the "biggest inflections of our lifetime." "We try to anticipate what will make customers' lives easier and better every day, and invent the next inflection," Jassy wrote. Analysts also expect the humanoid market to surge in the coming years. Barclays forecast in a January report that the global market, which it currently values at $2 billion to $3 billion, could reach roughly $40 billion by 2035, or as high as $200 billion "under the most optimistic scenarios." Earlier this year, Amazon redeployed much of the team behind Astro and brought in an MIT roboticist to work on the home robot project, LinkedIn profiles show. It also made a splashy acquisition to supercharge the effort. In March, Amazon scooped up New York-based Fauna Robotics, which has built a 3.5-foot-tall humanoid called Sprout. At the time, the company said Fauna would become part of a new division dubbed the Personal Robotics Group. Some Personal Robotics Group staffers previously worked in Amazon's Lab126 R&D unit, which has been behind many of Amazon's most successful consumer hardware products, like the Kindle e-reader, Echo smart speakers, Fire TV and Fire Tablet. Lab126 was also behind one of Amazon's biggest flops, the Fire Phone. It's unclear what kind of home robot the group is developing, or the types of tasks it could handle, but a June job posting hinted at an effort to "create robots that are not just functional, but delightful." Amazon could be looking to adapt Fauna's robots for homes or businesses. The Sprout humanoid, which was designed to be "friendly and capable" with expressive yellow eyebrows, has primarily been used by developers, as well as commercial and academic researchers. An Amazon job posting published online in October describes a "Field Support Engineer" who can assist with customer support and on-site repair, while another listing seeks a user experience designer to "define what it feels like to live with a Fauna robot." "Our goal is simple: make robots people actually want to live and interact with in everyday human spaces," the listing states. Amazon spokesperson Brad Glasser told CNBC in a statement that the company acquired Fauna because it's "committed to tackling the challenges that can unlock the personal robotics category." "We're optimistic about a future where personal robots are helping people in meaningful ways in everyday life, and we intend to play an important role in making that future a reality," Glasser said. Glasser noted that there remains a substantial gap between what's possible in a controlled lab and what's possible in settings like the living room or a lobby. Amazon is working with the robotics community to solve these challenges, he said. Emily Lugo Velez has been living with the Astro in her North Carolina home since 2023. Lugo Velez, who worked in IT and now runs an AI advisory business, said she and her husband weren't fazed by the robot's $1,000-plus price tag and quickly joined the waitlist. "We spent so much money on this thing," Lugo Velez, 52, said in an interview. "I feel like we're just stuck with it, and we'll let it run around the house until it eventually dies, then send it to the trash heap." She said she still uses the device to check on her pets and appliances when she's out of the house. But beyond that, Astro has primarily become a party trick and a "trip hazard." Most days, she tells Astro to go back to its charging dock. Executives who worked on Astro had discussed making it more capable by attaching an arm to pick up and inspect items without breaking them, said Ken Washington, who served as Amazon's VP of consumer robotics until 2023. He told CNBC that he pushed for a bipedal robot, but leadership disagreed. "We had Jeff [Bezos] in for show and tells and reviews, and I watched his body language pretty closely," Washington said. "I think he was disappointed with the lack of functionality, but I think he was impressed with its ability to map and navigate an undefined space under all lighting conditions." For all the struggles with Astro, Amazon has a rich history in robotics. The company acquired Kiva Systems for $775 million in 2012, which introduced mobile robots to its vast fulfillment network. Since then, Amazon's warehouse automation efforts have ballooned to over one million robots across its facilities that can pick, sort and ferry items to workers. But homes offer unique obstacles for robots to navigate. "The home is a completely different space," said Jeff Burnstein, president of the trade group Association for Advancing Automation, who has been in the robotics industry for 45 years. "Children, pets, grandparents, stairways. Nobody's home is set up exactly the same, so it's a much more challenging environment for a robot, certainly a robot that's walking." Amazon may have more luck its second time around because the tools for building robots have advanced by "leaps and bounds" over the past few years, said Colin Angle, a co-founder and former CEO of Roomba maker iRobot. Amazon attempted to acquire iRobot in 2022 before walking away from the deal two years later amid growing regulatory pushback. "The toolkit that the Astro team had when they did it was clubs with nails in them, just incredibly primitive," Angle said. "It's difficult to understate just how much the robot industry has changed in the last two years." Advances in AI models, sensors, battery systems and key mechanical components like actuators have spurred a new wave of development around robots for industrial and consumer use. Elon Musk's Tesla has been developing its bipedal Optimus robots since 2021. Startups including Apptronik, Boston Dynamics, China's Unitree, Figure and 1X are also building humanoids. Agility Robotics, the company behind the bipedal Digit robot that counts Amazon as one of its backers, went public via a SPAC on Thursday. Venture capital firms poured $33.4 billion into robotics and physical AI companies in the first half of the year, compared with $28.7 billion for all of 2025, according to PitchBook data. Most humanoids are being developed with the manufacturing, logistics and healthcare industries in mind, but a growing group of companies are attempting to build robots for the home. Apple is reportedly working on several home robot projects, including a tabletop device that resembles the Pixar lamp. Hugging Face, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for almost $13 billion in September, released the $399 Microduck in August. Angle, in May, launched a startup building fuzzy companion robots called Familiar Machines & Magic. Companies including Sunday, Tau and Nori claim their robots can help with household chores like folding laundry and clearing the table, but they remain mostly prototype or niche devices. "[Astro] was so ahead of its time," Washington said. "It was such a big, massive leap that I felt like we had the right to own the home." The robot's limited functionality and its $1,000-plus price tag likely made it a tough sell for many consumers, said a former Amazon employee who worked on Astro, who asked not to be named in order to speak frankly about the project. "Our poor little Astro was around $2,000 when it came out, and that's a lot," the ex-employee said. "That's a lot for a consumer, and they want a robot that does a lot." Amazon takes a long term view on new markets like personal robotics, and values what can be gained by being an early entrant, Glasser said. Astro was designed to help Amazon build competencies and focus its ambition, he added. The company has applied many of the learnings, talent and experience from Astro into its other robotics efforts, Glasser said. In Facebook groups for Astro owners, users have complained of diminished customer service and griped that Amazon's AIexa+ AI assistant isn't supported on Astro. Some users have interpreted this to mean Astro could be discontinued. Others have tried to dump their units at a discount on eBay and Facebook Marketplace. Glasser said Amazon continues to support Astro customers. Joe Martin, an Astro owner who lives near Tucson, Arizona, said he feels he's gotten his money's worth out of the device over the past four years. He'd welcome another robot into his home if it could do more, like helping out around the house. "Astro was $1,000 and it was pretty limited, but if it could bring a drink to me or dust furniture, I'd be intrigued by that," Martin, 65, said. "I think that's right around the corner."

articles.content: Presidentti Sauli Niinistö totesi Ylen Ykkösaamussa lauantaina , että Venäjän hybridivaikuttamiseen täytyisi luoda vastapaino. Hän vertasi tarvetta kylmän sodan kalseimpiin vuosiin, jolloin supervaltojen välisessä ydinasekilvassa vallitsi kauhun tasapaino. Hybridioperaatioihin vastaaminen samalla mitalla on eurooppalaisille valtioille vaikeaa, koska vieraan maan kansalaisten arkeen vaikuttavaa kiusantekoa pidettäisiin rikollisena. Yhdysvaltojen ja Britannian tiedustelupalvelut, agenttitarinoista tutut CIA ja MI6, ovat kuitenkin kansalliseen turvallisuuteen vedoten tehneet peiteoperaatioita. Niinistön mukaan linkki näihin laitoksiin on Euroopalle arvokas. Politiikan, talouden ja oikeuden suhdetta tutkiva Helsingin yliopiston yliopistotutkija Timo Miettinen on samaa mieltä Niinistön kanssa siitä, että hybridi-iskuihin pitäisi jollain tavalla vastata. – Suhtaudun kuitenkin varauksella siihen, että kaikkiin Venäjän toimiin pitäisi vastata ikään kuin samalla mitalla. Miettisen mielestä Venäjälle pitää tehdä selväksi, että sen tihutöillä on seurauksia. – Euroopan etu on, että meillä on käytössämme muitakin tapoja kuin mitä Venäjä on valinnut. Tavat ovat lähinnä Venäjään kohdistuvia pakotteita, joita Eurooppa on jo toistakymmentä vuotta asettanut. Miettinen ei usko, että pakotteilla käännettäisiin Venäjän politiikan suunta, mutta niiden pitkäaikaisempi vaikutus tuntuu muualla. – Pakotteiden ensisijainen tarkoitus tässä tilanteessa on yleisesti heikentää Venäjän toimintakykyä siten, että se joutuisi nojaamaan enemmän vaikka kiinalaiseen tai muuhun teknologiaan. Miettinen muistuttaa Niinistön vuonna 2024 laatimasta EU:n kokonaisturvallisuusraportista, jossa juuri Euroopan monipuolinen kyky vastata Venäjän hybridiuhkiin nähtiin vahvuutena. – Niinistökin nähdäkseni totesi siinä raportissa, että epäsymmetriset vastaukset ovat yleensä kuitenkin tehokkaampia kuin suora silmä silmästä -toiminta. EU:n jäsenmailla on Miettisen mukaan erilaisia näkemyksiä tilanteesta. Yksittäiset uhkat saattavat kuulua enemmän kansallisen turvallisuuden piiriin, jolloin kaikki maat eivät ole välttämättä sitä mieltä, että hybridivaikuttaminen ylipäätään on EU:n yhteinen asia. Miettinen arvelee, että Euroopan maat haluaisivat kyetä vastaamaan Venäjän kiusantekoon nykyistä vahvemmin. Historia saattaa kuitenkin estää pyrkimykset. – Esimerkiksi Saksan perustuslaissa on aika tiukkojakin lukkoja sen suhteen, että minkä tyyppisiä turvallisuusoperaatioita omien rajojen ulkopuolella voidaan suorittaa. Ehkä Ranskalla perinteisesti nämä kyvykkyydet tämän tyyppisissä asioissa ovat olleet vahvempia.

Instead, Miettinen advocates ruthless, data-driven financial enforcement, proving that algorithmic supply-chain asphyxiation degrades the Kremlin's defense-industrial base far more permanently than isolated digital counterstrikes.

articles.title: Mainstream Media Pioneers Deploy Generative AI Utility Applications
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens , the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale stems. It highlighted this sweet, funny relationship between a media brand’s personalities and its audience, a warm-casual vibe. I am not among the multitudes in the Cooking section's commenter army, but a few days later I was very surprised to see some of them in open revolt. I was even more surprised to see why: In an iOS-only beta, the Times is now using AI to allow subscribers to modify recipes. Below the article announcing the change on October 23, commenters loudly aired their grievances, threatening to cancel subscriptions, asking who wanted this, and how to turn it off. After four days and 172 almost exclusively angry comments, commenting for the story was turned off. The Times doesn't share Cooking's subscriber numbers, but NYT executive communications director Jordan Cohen said the site and app were visited 514 million times in 2025, and its YouTube channel has over 1.4 million subscribers. Reading over the section's AI plans and thinking about how many bungled attempts I'd seen to mush technology into places where it doesn't need to be in the kitchen, I guessed that I would side with the commenters. Then I tried the new AI feature, and found that it worked surprisingly well. My writing for WIRED over the past decade has shown me again and again that adding tech to a kitchen product is risky at best. I've repeatedly watched companies try and fail: Bluetooth connections for all the appliances, apps that lean too heavily on crummy recipes, toasters with optical sensors or touchscreens that still couldn't toast particularly well. Just about anything that was part of the "smart kitchen" tended not to be very smart at all. Developing dependable, delicious recipes is hard, expensive work that can require a whole staff. Yet skimping can hurt the brand. Two notable companies with a deep bench—The New York Times Cooking and America's Test Kitchen—are cooking content makers. Recipes, which is to say delicious, high-quality, tested recipes, are what they do. Since AI is often a lousy chef , giving it a role in the presentation of NYT's gold mine of content is a big risk. If you want to make banana bread but tell it you don't have a loaf pan, it'll ask you what kind of pans you do have, then modify the recipe to suit. All the changes throughout the recipe are noted in a visible red-orange text. Over several days of testing, I saw how you can do relatively simple things like swap ground pork for ground beef, or make more complicated demands like asking it to tailor things to your dietary needs. The modifications it makes are very visible throughout the recipe. If you ask it for something too out there—like turning Eric Kim's gochujang buttered noodles into a cookie—it gives you a "hard redirect" and points you to a better-suited recipe, which in this case is Kim's gochujang caramel cookies . Courtesy of New York Times For its recommendations, the LLM looks at the recipe itself, the Times’ ingredient substitution guide , user comments, and then what it calls AI "drawing on our expertise," in that order. Velasquez says the AI should be a helper, not the main act, noting, "You shouldn't be chatting with it." She explains that when the Times built the AI functionality, recipe editors helped create the original rule set, then evaluated how it worked at the end. When I ask what this means for the jobs of 60 editors, writers, video journalists, and other employees—the team that creates the recipes people use and curates the vibe readers relate to—Velasquez stresses that NYT Cooking has been "hiring more than ever" and that it has "zero intention of publishing fewer recipes." So far, she says people are mainly using it for ingredient and equipment substitutions, along with adjusting recipes for dietary needs. "Some people use the chatbot to scale, or they'll scale to match an ingredient," giving the example of someone who had only one cup of oil for a recipe that needed more. As a food writer whose career has taken some substantial turns due to AI recently, I wouldn't say I've been clamoring for this, but I find the Times’ measured approach works pretty well. I started testing it out by making chicken and dumplings using a five-star Alison Roman recipe with more than 6,000 ratings. I asked the AI tool to swap out bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs for boneless, skinless breasts. It thought about it for a moment—"simmering" in AI Cooking patois—and then offered up "Chicken Breast and Dumplings," with the "breast" in the title rendered in the red-orange color that indicates a modification. Just below the title, it said it was "Joseph's version made with AI. Not tested or endorsed by the original recipe's creators." Along with those visible changes, I could also toggle back and forth between my version and the original. It all made sense except for one bit. It suggested the shredded, cooked breast go back into the pot for about another 30 minutes while the sauce thickens and the dumplings cook. I saw this coming and, well, I wasn't going to do that to my dinner. I put a handful of shredded meat in as directed so I could see what happened and reserved the rest. The shredded bits that were in for that extra half hour weren’t bad per se, but their texture was notably less succulent than what I'd reserved and way less than thighs would be. This was the largest issue I encountered in all of my testing. If I had been the creator of the Times' original recipe, I'm not sure how I'd feel about the option to use a breast instead of thighs, which is not unheard of, but not very common in classic chicken and dumpling recipes. Perhaps it's something that could be fine-tuned or simply not offered as an option. From there, it was fairly smooth sailing. I had it turn a Francis Lam roasted mushroom and broccoli grain bow l into a roasted mushroom, cauliflower, and squash grain bowl. The crucifer crisscross was an easy one-to-one, but I also told it to add a pound of delicata squash. It had me slice the squash into half moons so everything would finish at the same time, then upped the total amount of olive oil. Lam's poetic voice was preserved in both versions of the recipe, telling you to heat the olive oil "until it slips around the pan like water" before adding beaten eggs for festive dish-topping egg ribbons. My buddy Dave had come by for cribbage night, and this made for an enjoyable, healthy, pregame dinner before he went on to skunk me twice. into a yeasted version, which, unlike the original, gets an overnight in the fridge, letting the active dry yeast get bubbly and add an appealing tang. A friend suggested Colu Henry's pasta and chickpea stew. I swapped canned diced tomatoes I had in my pantry for whole, and asked it to "add more vegetables." It gave options in line with the recipe—carrots, celery, onion, zucchini, mushrooms, and extra greens—then put what I chose into the right spots throughout the procedure so everything went in at the right time. It made for a healthy, hearty dinner. Having been to the Portland Fermentation Festival recently and wanting guidance on incorporating a few extra ingredients, particularly garlic, into my sauerkraut, I used the AI to modify Lidey Heuck's original , saying "add carrots, garlic, and kale," which it suggested grating, thin slicing, and mincing, respectively, all in the right-feeling proportions. It also added more salt, since I was making more kraut. The big jar is sitting next to me as I type, and while it's several days from being ready, a sniff test tells me it's on its way to being a good batch. Finally, I turned Sue Li's peanut noodles with spicy tofu into peanut udon with tofu, whitefish, and cucumber. I started by asking it to make the original less spicy, add veggies, and "keep the tofu," but add some good-looking rockfish I found at the grocery store. Impressively, since the fish was an add-on, it had me cook it, then set it aside and wipe out the pan (!) before cooking the tofu. Since I swapped udon for the original bucatini, it customized the noodle-cooking guidance, too. Instead, it's saving us a trip to the store, or helping us use something we have on hand, or making it gluten-free, serving as a good and rare example of how you can use technology to make a product incrementally better. It also sounds like the commenters’ concerns have been heard. Velasquez let me know right away when we spoke that people will be able to hide the AI feature in the app if they want. The Times is also keeping the whole thing in iOS-only beta for now, and not saying when it would be available on other platforms. That bond that you can see between the Cooking team and its users is a pretty sweet thing. Deep down, I'm guessing the upset Cooking commenters felt worried they were going to lose some of that human connection. I hope it never goes away.

articles.title: Texas Localities Weaponized Zoning Against Power-Hungry Datacenters
articles.content: I turned to Alexis de Tocqueville, having read about him for years and never actually read him myself, after the Nov. 3 midterms handed Democrats a “blue tsunami” the likes of which I haven’t seen in my 43 years. Texas went blue down the line. And in 40 of 41 local votes across 10 states , Americans chose to limit data centers. Recommended Video Within days, $3.2 trillion of AI-related stock market wealth was wiped out as investors bet the election winners would slow the AI buildout. Texas holds one-fifth of the planned data-center pipeline , and its governor-elect has promised to ban new approvals until the state legislature acts. I had been privately skeptical, because data centers are the bedrock of the massive industrial boom powering most of America’s GDP growth. From an economic perspective, being anti-data center is like being pro-recession, I assumed, but Tocqueville’s Democracy in America explains a lot of what has really gone on in America for centuries. Tocqueville was a young French aristocrat who toured the United States in 1831 and published Democracy in America in two volumes, dated 1835 and 1840. The Library of America calls it arguably “the most perceptive and influential book ever written about American politics and society.” One big idea he offered was what he called the “ general equality of condition ” among Americans, meaning how widely property and status were spread around. And this, he proposed, is the fact that the rest of American life comes out of. He argued that Americans hold tight to their property, care more about equality than liberty, and organize locally to get what they want. The data-center industry made its plans without accounting for any of that, and it’s an open question whether the Democrats who just won a landslide really understand it, themselves. Most Gen Xers can barely remember a wave like this one. The closest historical comp is the 1974 blue wave that swept aside the corruption of the Nixon Watergate era. The 2026 midterms suggest a scrambling of the calculus of red states and blue states much like Donald Trump’s shocking election did a decade ago, when the “ blue wall ” of Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Michigan crumbled. Nationally, Democrats have so far flipped seven Senate seats and are on track for at least 258 House seats . They took a majority of governors’ mansions for the first time since 2010 , and Trump acknowledged that Democrats had secured both chambers. Down the ballot, voters in 10 states decided 41 local measures on data centers , and in 40 of the 41 they favored limits on development . In NBC’s exit poll, 76% said they would oppose a new data center in their community . There were many stunners, like Kansas electing its first Democratic senator since 1932 , but Texas stands out as the signature shock. The Lone Star state went blue across its statewide offices. Beyond the Senate and governor’s races, Democrats won agriculture commissioner, attorney general, land commissioner, comptroller, lieutenant governor and railroad commissioner . They have taken the state House for the first time since 2002 . Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott and will be the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990 , and the first ever Hispanic person to hold the office. The Texas House looks likely to have its first female and first Black speaker in the form of 87-year-old Senfronia Thompson , who took office in 1973. Reading Tocqueville in this climate is downright spooky. He wrote in 1835 that American political bickering at first looks to a stranger “so incomprehensible and so puerile” that he can’t decide whether to pity the people or envy the happiness that lets them argue. I personally thought as much for months about the issue of data centers — a massively overstated environmental risk but a massively understated political and emotional issue — until voters proved they were not messing around. Look closer, Tocqueville wrote, and nearly every faction of American political life comes down to one side trying “to limit,” and the other “to extend, the popular authority.” Five years later, in his second volume, he explained what made Americans different from the Europeans watching them. “The great advantage of the Americans is that they have arrived at a state of democracy without having to endure a democratic revolution; and that they are born equal, instead of becoming so.” Two centuries on, that birthright came out on Nov. 3 as a mass of voters told the Republican Party, and the data-center builders, something like “No, I don’t think so.” Property, unlike aristocratic Europe where it is passed down from along family lines for centuries, is what keeps the whole thing from flying apart for most Americans, who are “possessed of sufficient property to desire the maintenance of order, yet not enough to excite envy.” Tocqueville observed that “the passions engendered by property are keenest and most tenacious amongst the middle classes.” And because equality leaves each person weak on his own, Americans band together to form what he called “associations,” without which they “become powerless if they do not learn voluntarily to help one another.” Tocqueville also prophesied that Texas would hold the key to the American future. “The inhabitants of the United States are perpetually migrating to Texas, where they purchase land; and although they conform to the laws of the country, they are gradually founding the empire of their own language and their own manners,” he wrote, a decade before Texas joined the Union. Texas has spent the 2020s proving him right. It added 391,243 residents in the year to July 2025, more than any other state for the third year in a row, reaching 31.7 million. It produced $2.9 trillion in GDP in 2025, and holds one-fifth of the planned 253-gigawatt data center pipeline nationwide. The five fastest-growing American cities , the Census Bureau revealed in May, were all in Texas, some for the second year running. This year, Texas put every one of Tocqueville’s arguments on the ballot at once. Landowners fought transmission lines after a 2023 law cut the time regulators have to consider them from 365 days to 180 . Groups like Save Rural Texas organized against data centers, and while Abbott ordered an audit of every data center in the grid queue , Hinojosa called for a statewide moratorium, vowing days before the vote to “stop the data center takeover.” Then the voters made clear in resounding fashion how they felt about property, equality and popular authority. , property and associations in the 21st century For a lot of voters this year, equality came down to the cost of living. In Gallup’s final preelection survey , 44% of voters called income and wealth distribution extremely important, the highest reading in the three midterms Gallup has measured it, up from 32% in 2018 and 31% in 2014. On PJM, the grid running from Illinois to New Jersey, the independent market monitor puts data centers at $6.3 billion of the latest auction’s $16.4 billion in capacity charges , and at $29.4 billion, or 46%, across the last four auctions. In the October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll , 57% of Americans called home energy and utility costs unaffordable, up from 45% in February. On property, Tocqueville wrote that “the heart of man is not so much caught by the undisturbed possession of anything valuable as by the desire, as yet imperfectly satisfied, of possessing it, and by the incessant dread of losing it.” The data-center fears, environmental concerns aside, cut straight to the American dread of losing one’s property. In August, a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found 57% of Texas voters opposed a data center in their community, including 43% of Republicans and 60% of rural voters . The other side claims property, too. Texas Policy Research , a free-market think tank, argues Texas should protect private property rights and free enterprise while making large electricity users pay the costs they impose on the grid. The “associations” that Tocqueville observed were so obvious in this election season they hardly need mentioning. Data Center Watch , a tracker maintained by AI research firm 10a Labs, counted 833 opposition groups across 49 states by March 2026, up from 396 at the end of 2025. In June, Seattle’s city council voted unanimously for a one-year ban , making it the largest U.S. city to pass one. None of these ran through Washington. Tocqueville spelled out the lesson in 1840: Americans describe their civic life in terms of self-interest. “The Americans… are fond of explaining almost all the actions of their lives by the principle of interest rightly understood,” he wrote. “They show with complacency how an enlightened regard for themselves constantly prompts them to assist each other.” When they do something public-spirited, in other words, they insist it is in their own interest. They “seldom allow that they yield to emotions of this kind; they are more anxious to do honor to their philosophy than to themselves.” He didn’t mean that as an insult, calling the principle “the best suited of all philosophical theories to the wants of the men of our time,” and “their chief remaining security against themselves.” That’s what most readings of the data-center fight, including mine, missed. From outside it looks like people guarding their power bills and their land. Others suspected the opposition was manufactured, even from China. The experts Fortune spoke to in June found it organic, with little evidence to support claims of China’s interference . The people in the fight talk about bills and property, as Tocqueville said they would, and they organized and voted in 41 places. Americans misread themselves on the bigger question, too. Before the vote, fewer than half expected free and fair midterms , according to a University of California, San Diego, survey. Experts weren’t much sunnier. In Bright Line Watch’s October survey , their median forecast of a free and fair election was 75%, and one article in Political Science Quarterly argued the country had descended into soft competitive authoritarianism . But Tocqueville reasoned in the chapter “Why Great Revolutions Will Become More Rare” that a country of small owners has too much to lose to blow itself up. “Nations are less disposed to make revolutions in proportion as personal property is augmented and distributed amongst them,” he wrote. Americans’ revolutions come through the ballot box when equality feels threatened. The contrast with Germany and France, where disaffected Gen Zers’ protests have turned violent in the streets , looks straight out of the late 18th century. Democrats would be making a Tocqueville-sized mistake to read Nov. 3 as a conversion. The border counties that swung toward them had swung the other way two years earlier. In 2024, Trump won all four counties in the Rio Grande Valley, a region Democrats had swept in almost every presidential election since at least the 1920s. In Texas, where Democrats won their largest House majority since the 1993 session, several Democratic flips were decided by mere hundreds of votes. In Kansas, Hamilton won as an “ independent-minded Democrat .” He avoided association with national Democrats and said he wouldn’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer for another leadership position, even though his campaign took $5 million from a PAC associated with Schumer. The voters who elected them were following the bills, the land and the town meeting and will surely follow them again. Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. articles.title: Arkansas Bar Exam Database Tampering Exposes Critical Insider Threat
articles.content: From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday : Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust. The full statement from the court: An internal review by Robert Brech, Executive Director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas's Office of Professional Conduct and Programs, has uncovered extensive irregularities involving the Court's Office of Professional Programs and the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. The matter was turned over to state and federal authorities. As of today, the Prosecuting Attorney's Office for the Sixth Judicial District filed formal criminal charges against Nancie Givens for 65 counts of tampering with a public record under Arkansas Code Annotated section 5-54-121 in connection with the alleged altering of numerous Arkansas Bar Examination scores and the deletion of files purportedly intended to conceal that misconduct. The charges followed a criminal investigation initiated in April 2026 by the Arkansas State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. As always, all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Moving forward, we are committed to holding those involved accountable, taking continued corrective oversight of the Arkansas Bar Examination, and determining the appropriate course of action. * * * * * In February 2026, Givens, the former Executive Director of this Court's Office of Professional Programs, resigned. At that time, Robert Brech was serving as Executive Director of the Court's Office of Professional Conduct. Following Givens's resignation, the Court directed Brech to supervise the Office of Professional Programs, which oversees the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. Upon his review of the Office of Professional Programs' records and administrative operations, Brech discovered that a large number of files and electronic communications were modified or deleted in early January 2026. Approximately 11,400 files were deleted or rendered unavailable. Most of those files included Arkansas Bar examinee applications, profiles, and examination score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by this Court's rules to retain for twenty-five years. Brech immediately notified a member of this Court, who directed him to determine the extent of the missing records and identify any other irregularities. On the basis of his review of the remaining files, Brech identified numerous discrepancies involving Arkansas Bar Examination scores across at least eight test administrations between July 2020 and July 2025. At that time, the matter was referred to the appropriate state and federal authorities. Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust. The vast majority of examinees who were previously informed that they had passed the Arkansas Bar Examination by the Office of Professional Programs did, in fact, pass the exam. Those examinees affected will be notified by the Office of Professional Conduct as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status. The Court is working with state and federal authorities to recover deleted and missing data, analyze all test administrations within that time frame, and determine the full scope of this grave and potentially criminal abuse of power. The people of Arkansas deserve, and the Court is committed to providing, total transparency in this matter. However, further disclosure will be forthcoming in a manner so as to not compromise the ongoing state and federal criminal investigations. Accordingly, additional disclosures will be limited as those efforts remain underway. As an immediate step, independent of any state or federal criminal investigation or prosecution, Nancie Givens has been referred to the Office of Professional Conduct for investigation of extensive violations of the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct. See Ark. R. Prof. Conduct 8.1(a) & 8.4(a)-(e). Furthermore, new testing procedures and security measures were implemented with the February 2026 administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination to ensure systemic accountability and safeguard the integrity of the examination. * * * * * We recognize the profound consequences for affected examinees, the Bar, and the public at large. Our paramount concern is safeguarding litigants, the integrity of the legal profession, and public confidence in the administration of justice. While these matters remain under criminal and administrative investigation, we commit to pursue continued corrective measures in an effort to reestablish confidence in our institution.

articles.title: Canberra Halts Defense Land Selloff to Retain Sovereign Enclaves
articles.content: The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Victoria Barracks Sydney held a ‘special place in our nation’s history’ after it and three other properties were removed from the government’s planned property sell-off. Photograph: CPL Dustin Anderson/AP View image in fullscreen The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Victoria Barracks Sydney held a ‘special place in our nation’s history’ after it and three other properties were removed from the government’s planned property sell-off. Photograph: CPL Dustin Anderson/AP Four heritage-listed defence properties to be preserved for community use after backlash from veterans and former PMs Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Richard Marles has denied claims Australia’s defence will be undermined by its decision to repurpose a historical military base near Sydney’s CBD for public use. The Albanese government announced on Sunday four heritage-listed defence sites, including Sydney’s Victoria Barracks, will remain in public hands after the plan generated considerable public backlash against their sale. Critics, including veterans and high-profile politicians such as former prime ministers John Howard and Paul Keating, fiercely opposed the decision, with some political opponents questioning if the country’s largest city would be more vulnerable to foreign military and terrorist attacks. The defence minister said the buildings were mostly used by office workers and no one was “seriously” suggesting the convict-labour built Victoria Barracks was fundamental to Australia’s defence. “People making the argument know that. I don’t think there’s anyone who’s really seriously suggesting this facility is fundamental to the defence of Australia.” The defence-owned heritage sites, along with 63 others around the country, were identified in an independent audit as being underutilised by defence, not fit for purpose and costly to maintain, and were earmarked for sale to recoup $3bn in the federal budget. Albanese government to sell off $3bn worth of historic defence sites amid push to free up space for new homes Read more Ahead of an important cabinet meeting on the budget on Monday, the Albanese government confirmed that four sites – Victoria Barracks in Sydney and Melbourne , and Fort Queenscliff and RAAF Base Point Cook in Victoria – will remain publicly owned and their historic elements preserved for community use after they are vacated by defence personnel. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese , said parts of the soon-to-be publicly owned sites could still be used for commercial purposes, in line with heritage laws, to help cover their maintenance costs. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The government will work with the Australian War Memorial once the sites are free to transform the sites into public spaces that tell the history of Australia’s military. Sydney’s Victoria Barracks was built between 1840 and 1848 and was originally occupied by the British army. It is also the site of the city’s oldest wine cellar. The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said questions remain about whether the military should have more of a presence and capability in Melbourne and Sydney. “While this is a win for Australia’s defence heritage, it is only the beginning. The Coalition will continue to fight to save other critical defence sites, including HMAS Penguin, Lancer Barracks, Irwin Barracks, and more,” he said. The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the site was an “irreplaceable part of our military heritage that deserves to be protected for future generations”. “Our military heritage and defence capability must come before a short-term cash grab,” she said. The Returned & Services League of Australia president, Peter Tinley, said the announcement was a “partial victory”. “Retaining Victoria Barracks Sydney has never just been about its history. It’s home to the headquarters of forces command, and reservists and cadets train there. That’s a story that should be kept alive. Two other sites will be partially divested, the government announced. HMAS Penguin in Sydney’s northern beaches will be partially retained by defence with the Angophora Forest transferred to the Sydney Harbour Federation Trust. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion In the Northern Territory, the Stokes Hill fuel installation will be handed back to the Larrakia people, the traditional owners of the lands. The southern portion of the site is a registered sacred site and is protected under law. The multi-year audit, completed in 2023, was tasked with identifying surplus and costly property holdings, often costing millions to maintain. View image in fullscreen Victoria Barracks in Melbourne. The sales of the Sydney and Melbourne Victoria Barracks had been expected to raise $1.3bn, given their prime locations in the biggest capital cities. Photograph: Michael Currie/AAP The audit found 67 underutilised sites are “draining resources from higher priority needs” for defence. Off limits to Sydneysiders for more than a century, secretive Spectacle Island is coming up for sale Read more The sales of the Sydney and Melbourne Victoria Barracks were expected to raise $1.3bn, given their prime locations in the biggest capital cities. Up to $2.4bn was expected to be raised from the sale of 26 major metropolitan sites, saving about $3bn in upkeep and security costs over 10 years. These include sites in Randwick, Sydney; Sandringham and St Kilda in Melbourne; Petrie Terrace in Brisbane; and Fremantle in Western Australia. The government hopes the sales will free up land for new housing developments with a long-term target of 6,000 new dwellings. Defence expects personnel will have vacated six sites by the end of the year and all sites to be divested from within two years. The announcement comes as cabinet’s expenditure review committee, which determines budget decisions, meets on Monday after the official interest rate was lifted to an 18-year high of 4.85% in a bid to combat persistent inflation this week. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said this week higher fuel prices due to the Middle East conflict were the “primary driver” of inflation rather than the government’s budget.
